transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-17
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Marco Ruiz; Priya Malhotra; Liam Chen; Sofia Alvarez; Raj Patel; Eve Park

[00:00:00] Marco Ruiz: hey everyone, thanks for joining. Marco from Redwood Inference, i'm the AE on this account. quick check on audio — can you hear me okay?
[00:00:06] Liam Chen: yes loud and clear, thanks Marco.
[00:00:09] Marco Ruiz: sweet. i put a quick agenda in the calendar: walk through JSON mode / structured output, show tool calling patterns, demo the console sandbox and then chat about pilot scope and security. we'll try to keep it tight.
[00:00:22] Sofia Alvarez: sounds good. we mainly want to see how we can enforce schemas and make tool calls deterministic for our enrichment flow.
[00:00:28] Priya Malhotra: great, i'll drive the demo portion. quick qual: what's your current stack for model serving and tooling?
[00:00:36] Liam Chen: right now everything is in-house — we run a mix of hosted endpoints on GCP with some custom microservices for enrichment. latency is... OK, but we see big variance during peak. also our security team prefers VPC-only solutions for PII workloads.
[00:00:49] Raj Patel: yeah and from security, we need KMS integration, audit logs, and SSO. SOC2 is in progress.
[00:00:55] Marco Ruiz: got it. that matches a lot of customers who move from hosted to either dedicated or private. today we'll show you both the hosted JSON-mode controls and how the private deployment supports the same contracts.
[00:01:06] Priya Malhotra: all right jumping in — opening the Redwood Console. i'll start with a quick JSON-mode example: imagine a content pipeline that needs a fixed schema for an enrichment call — entity extraction + sentiment + a flag to call an external enrichment tool when entities include 'company' or 'email'.
[00:01:26] [00:01:26] Priya Malhotra: (screen) here's a schema we author: fields are entities: array of {type,name,span}, sentiment: enum {positive,neutral,negative}, call_tool: boolean, tool_payload: object optional. you can pin validators and a fallback policy.
[00:01:41] Sofia Alvarez: quick q — can the schema enforce types deeply? like ensure tool_payload includes an 'source_id' as string and a 'priority' integer?
[00:01:50] Priya Malhotra: yep, nested validation supported. we also have typed coercion options, but you can choose strict mode to fail the response if it doesn't match.
[00:01:58] Liam Chen: when it fails, what's the runtime behavior? does it retry, or does it call the fallback?
[00:02:04] Priya Malhotra: good question — that's where guards and fallbacks come in. you can configure 'reject', 'auto-correct', or 'fallback'. reject will return an error to the caller, auto-correct will run a quick reformat pass, and fallback will route to a cheaper model variant or a non-structured path.
[00:02:20] Raj Patel: we need deterministic behavior for compliance — so likely reject and then surface an error to our pipeline for manual review.
[00:02:28] Marco Ruiz: totally makes sense. in Private deployments you get the same config and observability — token-level traces, schema mismatch histograms in the console.
[00:02:37] [00:02:37] Priya Malhotra: switching to tool calling. i'll show an example where the model returns a tool invocation payload, then Redwood runtime validates the schema and executes the tool in an isolated sandbox, with RBAC checks and audit events.
[00:02:52] Priya Malhotra: (screen) Here's the tool definition: enrichment_api_v1, auth: KMS-signed token, timeout 3s, retry policy 1. Notice you can map which fields flow into the tool request and which outputs are merged back into the top-level response.
[00:03:08] Sofia Alvarez: if the tool fails, can we configure fallback logic like 'try tool A, else tool B' or 'skip tool and annotate error'?
[00:03:16] Priya Malhotra: yes to both. we have tool chaining and conditional fallbacks. you can set a sequential fallback chain or a simultaneous race with latency thresholds.
[00:03:26] Liam Chen: what's the overhead on calling a tool from the runtime? i.e. latency delta for tool invocation vs pure LLM response.
[00:03:33] Priya Malhotra: depends on the tool endpoint — the runtime adds minimal orchestration (~10-20ms) plus network to the target. for internal services within the same VPC it's usually sub-50ms; for external SaaS it's variable. Redwood Optimize can recommend batching or prefetching to hide some of that latency.
[00:03:51] Raj Patel: can we run the tool execution inside our VPC for data egress control?
[00:03:56] Marco Ruiz: yes — in Private mode the runtime can run within your VPC and call internal endpoints without traffic leaving your network. tool secrets like API keys are stored in your KMS/HSM and signed on invocation.
[00:04:09] [00:04:09] Priya Malhotra: demo time — i'm going to send a sample text through the console playground. first the model returns a structured response that triggers a tool call.
[00:04:20] [00:04:20] (typing)
[00:04:28] Priya Malhotra: here's the output. notice the 'call_tool': true, and a 'tool_invocation' object with target tool and payload. the console shows an expanded trace: schema validation passed, tool dispatched, response merged.
[00:04:43] Sofia Alvarez: looks neat — the merged response shows entity scores we can use. question: are the tool outputs cached? we have deterministic enrichment that repeats across users.
[00:04:53] Priya Malhotra: yes, you can configure a caching key based on schema fields; the runtime will cache tool outputs for the TTL you specify. Redwood Optimize can recommend cache keys based on usage patterns.
[00:05:04] Liam Chen: and for cost control, can we force a cheaper model for fallback-only paths?
[00:05:09] Marco Ruiz: yes, you can route the fallback route to a smaller quantized model; the smart routing layer will pick the variant by policy. that reduces token cost when strictness isn't required.
[00:05:20] [00:05:20] Priya Malhotra: now i'll show the API side: the JSON-mode request includes a 'response_contract' header where you attach the schema id and a 'tool_policy' block. the API returns either a structured JSON or an error code with diagnostics.
[00:05:36] Liam Chen: how verbose are the diagnostics? we need something our SREs can parse automatically.
[00:05:41] Priya Malhotra: diagnostics come back as a compact list: mismatch_path, expected_type, observed_value, suggested_fix. there's also a trace id that you can feed to console logs for full token-level trace.
[00:05:52] Raj Patel: about logs — for audit we need immutable append-only logs for schema decisions. can those be exported to our SIEM?
[00:05:59] Marco Ruiz: yes, we support streaming audit logs to your Cloud Logging or to an S3-compatible endpoint with signed delivery. On Private you can keep all logs inside your network.
[00:06:10] [00:06:10] Sofia Alvarez: switching gears: our pipeline needs to run at 200 QPS during peak. what's your experience with throughput for schema-enforced invocations?
[00:06:21] Priya Malhotra: generally throughput is gated by model latency and tool latency. Redwood's serving runtime uses continuous batching and KV cache for prefix reuse; for 200 QPS we typically recommend dedicated pools with autoscaling and a warm KV cache profile. for many customers, a couple of reserved nodes with burst capacity handled this.
[00:06:40] Liam Chen: can you quantize models and keep schema checks? our models are sometimes custom.
[00:06:46] Priya Malhotra: yes, quantization is supported and we'll keep the same schema enforcement. if you bring a custom model, we do a compatibility pass; some quantization packs may slightly change token timing but the semantics are the same.
[00:06:59] Raj Patel: what about data residency — our EU customers require EU-only processing.
[00:07:04] Marco Ruiz: we have regional routing and Private deployments can be stood up in your region. the console shows per-region traces and you can pin a policy to restrict model variants to EU regions.
[00:07:15] [00:07:15] Priya Malhotra: demo: failure mode. i'll intentionally break the schema — remove required source_id from tool_payload. watch the runtime path.
[00:07:26] [00:07:26] (typing)
[00:07:33] Priya Malhotra: output shows schema mismatch, policy set to 'reject' so the API returns 422 with diagnostics. i can toggle to 'auto-correct' — it does a reformat pass and then re-evaluates; sometimes that saves an extra round trip.
[00:07:48] Sofia Alvarez: auto-correct worries us for compliance — we lose auditability if we modify user content. can we still log the before/after?
[00:07:56] Marco Ruiz: yes, all intermediate artifacts are logged with trace ids and can be exported. you can also disable auto-correct and enforce only 'reject' in production.
[00:08:07] [00:08:07] Liam Chen: OK, cost question — how do we estimate token changes we get from structured mode? our billing needs to map to merchant events.
[00:08:16] Marco Ruiz: billing is per-token for generations plus a small per-invocation fee for tool calls; cached tool outputs reduce per-call tokens. Redwood Optimize will run an analysis and produce a cost delta report for your sample data. we'll provide a sample spreadsheet.
[00:08:31] Raj Patel: on SLA and uptime — our legal team needs 99.95% for dedicated pools.
[00:08:37] Marco Ruiz: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed tiers; Private has enterprise SLAs in contracts. We'll include the SLA appendix in the pack we send.
[00:08:45] [00:08:45] Priya Malhotra: quick note about observability — console gives per-schema histograms, contract violation rates, and a replay sandbox where you can re-run past requests against model variants. that's great for root cause.
[00:08:58] Eve Park: could the replay be used in CI for model rollouts? we want to ensure rollbacks happen safely.
[00:09:04] Priya Malhotra: yes, many customers use an eval set + replay to gate rollouts. console integrates with canary policies so you can specify automatic rollback if contract violations exceed threshold.
[00:09:16] [00:09:16] Marco Ruiz: want to talk pilot? typical pilot we propose is a 2-week sandbox: we onboard a small dataset, wire up a sample tool endpoint (or your internal enrichment service in VPC), run perf tests, and produce a cost/latency report plus a small set of guardrail configs.
[00:09:33] Liam Chen: that sounds reasonable. timeline: we want to get something running in the next 2 weeks if possible.
[00:09:38] Marco Ruiz: great — actionables: i'll send the pilot template and pricing. Priya will run a perf run on your sample data. Raj will review security docs.
[00:09:46] Raj Patel: one more question — encryption-at-rest for cached tool outputs. are cached results encrypted with our KMS?
[00:09:52] Marco Ruiz: yes, in Private and Dedicated caches can be encrypted using your KMS keys; hosted uses Redwood-managed keys by default but you can bring your own key in many enterprise plans.
[00:10:03] [00:10:03] Priya Malhotra: wrapping up demo — i'll paste links to the console recording, the schema example, and a short how-to deck in the chat.
[00:10:12] (chat) Priya Malhotra: https://redwood.example.com/sandbox/rec/ff-azura-0917
[00:10:16] (chat) Marco Ruiz: pilot template: https://redwood.example.com/pilot-templates/json-invoke-pilot.pdf
[00:10:20] (chat) Marco Ruiz: security pack: https://redwood.example.com/security/azura-pack
[00:10:24] Liam Chen: perfect. we'll review and come back with proposed internal stakeholders.
[00:10:28] Eve Park: i can help schedule the kickoff. wave two questions — can we bring our own model weights?
[00:10:34] Priya Malhotra: yes, you can bring a custom model in Private or Dedicated. we run a compatibility and perf validation step, and then you can pin it in the console.
[00:10:45] [00:10:45] Marco Ruiz: final recap: send pricing + pilot template + security docs; run perf test; schedule sandbox kickoff next week.
[00:10:54] Liam Chen: thanks everyone.
[00:10:56] Marco Ruiz: thank you, talk soon.

(End of recording)
